title: Which design pattern would you use?
description: Short scenarios across all the families: read the need, name the pattern, and say why not the look-alike.

questions.text: You need to guarantee a single shared rate-limit counter service in a process, and tests must be able to replace it. What is the best approach?

options.text: A hard-coded Singleton with a static `Instance`
One instance created at startup and injected where needed

questions.explanation: The need is "one instance", which is a lifetime decision, not necessarily a Singleton class. Registering it as a single instance in the container keeps it replaceable in tests.

questions.text: A checkout must apply stackable extras (gift wrap, insurance, express) to any item, each optional, in any combination. Which pattern?
questions.explanation: Each extra wraps the item and adds to its price or description while keeping the same interface, so combinations come from stacking rather than from a subclass per combination.

questions.text: An app must show the same data as a table, a chart and a CSV, and new views will be added. Where should each view get its data?

options.text: Views subscribe to a model (Observer) or consume a common interface, and the data logic is written once
Each view inherits from every other view
A switch in the model for each view

questions.explanation: Separating the model from its views, with change notification, is the idea behind Observer and MVC. New views plug in without touching the model.

questions.text: You must support undo/redo in a text editor. Which pattern is the natural fit?

options.text: Command (with a history stack), possibly with Memento

questions.explanation: Each edit is a command with `execute` and `undo`; a stack of them gives undo and redo. Memento can store snapshots when reversing an action is hard.

questions.text: A legacy XML client must be used by new code that expects JSON-returning methods. Which pattern?
questions.explanation: The new code defines the interface it wants, and an adapter translates to the legacy client. Adapter is for mismatched interfaces; Facade is for simplifying one.

questions.text: Which is the best match for "give callers one simple method to place an order, while internally calling inventory, payment and shipping subsystems"?
questions.explanation: A facade presents a task-oriented API over several subsystem classes. It coordinates but does not change their interfaces.

questions.text: A cache that should be consulted before a slow service, with the same interface as the service. Which pattern describes the cache layer?
questions.explanation: A caching proxy shares the service's interface, intercepts the call, and only forwards on a miss. A decorator can look the same; the intent here is access control and cost.

questions.text: Which of these are good signals that Strategy is the right pattern?

options.text: You want to test each algorithm alone
The object must change behaviour as it moves through lifecycle states automatically
You see a long `if/else` choosing an algorithm by type
The same step has several interchangeable algorithms

questions.explanation: Interchangeable algorithms, type-switching and isolated testing all suggest Strategy. Behaviour that changes by itself through a lifecycle points to State.

questions.text: Using a pattern is always better than writing plain code, because patterns are proven.
questions.explanation: False. A pattern pays for itself only when the problem it solves is present. For a fixed two-case `if`, a pattern is extra indirection. Start with the simplest code and refactor to a pattern when the pain appears.

questions.text: Many `if (role == ...)` checks repeat before sensitive calls across the codebase. Which pattern moves them to one place?

options.text: Chain of Responsibility or a protection Proxy around the service

questions.explanation: A protection proxy or a middleware chain performs the check once, uniformly, before the call reaches the real service.
